blocks.text: Deputatov’s account follows Ignatius from military engineering through illness and discharge to four years as a novice. It singles out his bond with Leonid of Optina. It then relates the emperor’s intervention in his appointment to Saint Sergius Hermitage, and describes the twenty-four years spent rebuilding the community before episcopal consecration in 1857.

blocks.text: Retirement did not end the practical work described by the OCA. At Babaev he improved buildings, finances, the use of land, and the monastery’s internal order. The account also records visits from close associates and imperial visitors, including AlexanderII in 1866. It shows his final years combining revision of manuscripts, correspondence, and continuing responsibility for a community.

blocks.text: The same publication describes retirement after four years as bishop, the editing of earlier articles, and extensive correspondence with spiritual children. It identifies The Arena, the ascetical collections, the Patericon, and writing on death among the literary legacy. Its opening credits the translated selection to Deputatov’s The Awareness of God. The translated spiritual sayings that follow are not reproduced as if their English wording were public domain.

blocks.text:
Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.

Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.

Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.

Meditate upon these things; give thyself wholly to them; that thy profiting may appear to all.

Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee.
blocks.context: Related Scripture; not a claim that this passage narrates the saint’s life or is a prescribed feast-day reading.

blocks.text: Deputatov introduces the collected writings as material grounded in the Fathers. His account gives the English reader a bibliographic starting point while retaining the difference between an author’s life and a personalized ascetic program.
